title: Choose life (Deuteronomy 30:15–20)
hook: life and death set before you: choose life
carry: the word is very near you

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shema: hear, O Israel, and love God with heart, soul and strength. Your line was with all thy heart.

The day after Ash Wednesday, when Catholics have just had ashes on their foreheads and heard remember you are dust, the Church opens the Bible to this page. Moses is near the end of his last speech. He's given all the laws, the stories, the warnings. Now he does what a good teacher does at the end of a long course: he boils it down to one choice. Not a hundred rules. Two roads. And in front of witnesses, he tells them which one to take.
screen: `THE DAY AFTER ASH WEDNESDAY.` → `THE END OF MOSES'S SPEECH.` → `TWO ROADS.`

segments.voice: First, the nearness. Just before this, Moses says this commandment isn't too hard for you or far away. It isn't up in heaven, so that you'd need someone to go get it, and it isn't across the sea. The word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it. Second, the choice. "I call heaven and earth to witness this day, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing. Choose therefore life, that both thou and thy seed may live." Moses doesn't pretend there's no choice, and he doesn't make it for them. He lays both roads out plainly and then, like a parent, can't help saying which one he hopes they'll take. Third, what life means. In Hebrew, the word for life, chayyim, is plural, as if life were never just one thing; the toast l'chaim, to life, comes from it. And Moses says what that life is: loving the Lord, listening to his voice, holding fast to him, for he is your life and the length of your days. Choosing life, in Moses's words, isn't only staying alive. Fourth, how Catholics carry it. Pope John Paul the Second drew on passages like this in his letter on the Gospel of Life, teaching that every human life, from its beginning to its natural end, is a gift to protect. And the Church puts this reading at the start of Lent, a season of small choices, every one of them a road.
screen: `THE WORD IS VERY NEAR YOU.` · `LIFE AND DEATH, BLESSING AND CURSE.` · `CHAYYIM: LIFE, IN THE PLURAL.` · `HE IS THY LIFE.`

segments.voice: Look at the day ahead and find one small fork in it: bed on time or scrolling till two, calling your mother back or letting it go another week, the kind word or the sharp one. See both roads clearly, the way Moses laid them out, and choose the one with more life in it. If you pray, ask for help to keep that choice; if not, commit to it quietly.
Choose life. Moses's final charge: life and death set before you, and a plea to choose life, and the God who is life. Today's word.
Your line: the word is very near you. Close enough to choose today. Day three hundred eighty-eight, in the books.

howItsDone: Deuteronomy 30:15–20 is read at Mass on the Thursday after Ash Wednesday, at the start of Lent, and Pope John Paul II's encyclical Evangelium Vitae (1995) draws on it in teaching the dignity of every human life.

chat.says: When Moses says choose life, does he just mean stay alive?
options: More than that: loving God and holding fast to him, who Moses says is your life.
Yes, it's about avoiding danger so the people survive the desert.
He means choose a long life by keeping every rule perfectly.

notes: Thursday after Ash Wednesday: first reading Deuteronomy 30:15–20. Confirm.
Evangelium Vitae's use of Deuteronomy 30 (e.g., EV 28 and the encyclical's closing): stated generally as 'passages like this'. Confirm.
Chayyim as a plural form: standard grammar.
'Remember you are dust' at Ash Wednesday: one of the two formulas for the imposition of ashes.
